choices: The game is always played once
Players must move at exactly the same moment
One player moves after seeing the other's move
Each player decides without knowing the other's decision
explain: What matters is information: neither knows the other's choice. Moving after observing is sequential. One-shot versus repeated is a separate question.

stem: What does interdependence mean in game theory?
choices: Each player's payoff depends on the other players' choices
explain: A firm's best move depends on its rivals' moves.

stem: Which three elements make up a game?
explain: Who decides, what they can choose, and what each outcome pays.

stem: True or false: A one-shot game is played only once, while a repeated game is played more than once.
Why is game theory especially useful for oligopoly?
choices: Firms in oligopoly are price takers
A few firms' profits depend on each other's actions
explain: In perfect competition firms are too small to affect each other; a monopolist has no rival.

stem: Two construction firms submit sealed bids for a city contract. Neither sees the other's bid before the deadline. What kind of game is this?
explain: Sealed bids mean neither knows the other's choice; this contract is bid once.

stem: A grocery chain waits to see its rival's weekly ad before setting its own sale prices. What kind of game is this week's pricing decision?
explain: It observes the rival's choice before deciding.

stem: Visa and Mastercard each decide whether to lower merchant fees, without knowing what the other will announce. Why is game theory needed to predict Visa's choice?
choices: Visa's fee does not affect its profit
Visa's best fee depends on what Mastercard does
explain: Interdependence: each card network's profit depends on both fees.

stem: True or false: A simultaneous-move game is a game in which players make decisions without knowledge of the other players' decisions.
explain: True. It is about information, not the clock.

stem: Coke and Pepsi each set their summer prices in sealed plans sent to retailers on the same day. Later in the year they will set prices again. How should you model this summer's decision?
choices: A simultaneous-move game (one round of a repeated game)
explain: Neither sees the other's plan before committing. The yearly repetition makes it part of a repeated game (S20).

stem: Facebook and Twitter each decide in 2019 whether to ban political ads, without knowing the other's decision. In the Game Theory Exercise Part 1, how is this first modeled?
choices: As a sequential game with Twitter first
explain: Part 1 sets it up as a one-shot simultaneous game; Part 2 re-models it as a sequential game with Twitter moving first.
